summary:
This project aims to untangle the complex web of interactions between weather events and Earth’s systems by providing analysis tools and easy-to-understand, cute visualizations. We hope to empower anyone curious about the causes and effects of specific weather events.
Users describe a weather event in natural language, and our system identifies the relevant variables, time range, and location. Users can then apply our tools to perform time-series trend analysis with statistical significance testing.
We use coarse-resolution NASA data to remove seasonal and long-term trends, and fine-grained data to analyze the event itself.
details:
0. Github

https://github.com/oliiiiiiiiii/terra-trend

1. What It Does

Our tool is built for high school and university students, as well as researchers who want to explore Earth science. A user types in the weather or Earth event they want to investigate, then freely chooses a geographic area and a time period. Behind one easy-to-use web interface, the platform pulls from many different NASA datasets, so users can see how an event shows up in the data without needing to find, download, or process anything themselves.

2. How It Works

Users begin by typing the phenomenon they want to observe. If they are not sure where to start, the home page offers three example cases they can explore and learn from. Users then freely select the time period and the geographic region they care about. Based on the event they described, the system recommends the NASA variables most likely to be related to it, and users can accept or adjust the suggestions.

The platform then runs statistical analysis on the selected variables. It applies tests such as linear regression, the Mann–Kendall test, and the t-test, each reporting a p-value so users can tell whether a real trend exists instead of judging by eye. Additional tools help detect unusual behavior, such as flagging rare events, finding similar past cases, and forecasting. On the results page, users can adjust the time period again and switch between daily, weekly, and yearly data to see how the trend changes at different time scales. Next to the logo, three information pages explain how the platform works, including the analysis methods and detailed documentation of the datasets, so users can understand and check every step.

3. Benefits
  • Earth observation data is spread across many sources, formats, and units. Our platform brings these datasets together in one place and filters them down to the variables that actually relate to the user’s event. Analysis then happens in two steps:
  • Long-term trend: We start from the raw data and remove the seasonal cycle, which reveals the underlying long-term trend.
  • Residuals: We then remove both the seasonal cycle and the long-term trend from the raw data. What remains is the residual, which shows whether the event was unusual compared with normal conditions.
  • Users can read these two signals side by side. Below the main chart, a set of analysis tools (regression and more) helps them dig into the residuals and work out what kind of anomaly they are looking at.
4. Intended Impact

By combining data access, variable selection, and statistical analysis in one interface, we make real NASA data usable for people who are not data specialists. Our goal is to lower the barrier to doing scientific analysis, so that more students and members of the public can ask their own questions about the Earth system and build a stronger culture of scientific inquiry.

5. Innovation and Creativity

AI-guided variable selection. Most tools make users pick variables by hand, which requires knowing what to look for. Our system uses AI to judge which variables relate to the user’s event and recommends them. Users can still add or remove any of them.

Step-by-step presentation of two signals. We show the long-term trend and the residual separately, one step at a time. Users can see two different phenomena (a slow change and a sudden anomaly) instead of a single mixed curve.

6. Technical Details

We partition the Earth’s surface hierarchically. The globe is first split into land, ocean, and ice. Each domain is then divided into analysis units: HydroBASINS river basins at two levels on land, large marine ecosystems and named seas in the ocean, and the two ice sheets, plus a hexagonal grid that covers all three. In total there are about 7,600 regions. For every region, a preprocessing pipeline turns each dataset into a monthly time series and saves it in a small per-region file, so the website only loads the region the user picks. The 34 data layers come from IMERG, GRACE/GRACE-FO, GLDAS, MERRA-2, MODIS, and CERES, plus a few NOAA products that are labelled as non-NASA. They are grouped into 17 variable categories, such as precipitation, soil moisture, water storage, vegetation, temperature, and fire. For each category, a language model answers a yes/no question about whether it relates to the user’s event. By default this is Gemini 3.5 Flash on Vertex AI, and the local OneJev 1.6-0.8B model is also supported. A keyword table takes over if the model fails or takes longer than 5 seconds.

The monthly analysis runs in the browser. We fit a linear trend and a 12-month seasonal cycle on a baseline period, which is the full record minus a padding window around the event. The residual is the raw value minus the trend and the seasonal cycle. The z-score is the residual divided by the standard deviation of the baseline residuals. For the event window, we report the mean z-score and its percentile rank among all past windows of the same length. For the long-term trend, we report Sen’s slope with a 95% confidence interval and a Mann–Kendall test corrected for lag-1 autocorrelation. Below the chart, a test panel offers 24 more tools on the residual series: 17 statistical tests and 7 classical machine-learning methods. Examples are OLS, block bootstrap, Pettitt change-point, Lomb–Scargle periodogram, hidden Markov states, and Gaussian-process smoothing. When several tests run on the same range, Holm’s correction is applied. For short events, the server fetches daily GLDAS and IMERG values on demand from NASA OPeNDAP. The monthly trend and seasonal cycle are then interpolated to each day to remove them from the daily values. A batch mode answers many events from one CSV file. Missing values are never filled in or treated as zero. The app is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, three.js, and d3, and runs as one Docker container that includes the processed data.
